title: surge-efficiency-comparison-notes-apr21-2028
body:
Objective:
Run a compact, reproducible comparison of surge (short high-concurrency windows) efficiency across three serving strategies and two model variants. Focus: p50/p95/p99 latency, and amortized cost per 1k generated tokens under realistic two-turn chat workloads.

Summary / headline findings:
- Dynamic-sessionized batching with aggressive KV-cache prefetch gave the best p95/p99 behavior under short surges for conversational workloads, reducing p99 by ~18% vs fixed small batches and lowering cost/1k tokens by ~12% in our midrange scenario.
- Fixed-batch strategies maintained lower tail when workload is steady but cost blows up during microbursts due to wasted reserved slots.
- Quantized 4-bit model variant reduces per-token cost significantly (~30%) but increases p99 tail in high concurrency unless paired with session affinity.

Environment & workload:
- Models: rw-large-v1 (fp16) and rw-7b-q4 (4-bit quantized).
- HW pools: A100-80GB (core pool) and H100-80GB (edge trial).
- Traffic pattern: baseline 200 qps sustained for 10 minutes, then 5s surge pulses of 1200 concurrent requests every 30s for a 10-minute window (simulates chat app sync spikes).
- Request shape: 2-turn conversation. Prompt tokens 120 on average, generation 80 tokens. KV reuse expected across turns ~60% on average.
- Batching modes: fixed-batch-4 (slots of 4), dynamic-batch (fill-to-latency-target, continuous batching), sessionized (affinity + prefetch + KV cache hints).
- Cost metric: cloud-GPU compute-min normalized to cost units; report shows $ per 1k generated tokens using our internal unit conversion.

Methodology notes (short):
- Synthetic clients recorded RTT at client-observed entry and server-exit; server telemetry uses trace sampling to record kernel time, queue time, and KV cache hit rate.
- Each experiment run 5x; median across runs presented. 99ths computed from combined trace distribution.
- Warm caches for 2 minutes pre-surge to emulate warmed session cohorts; separate cold-run appendix available in linked artifacts.

Raw percentile table (median across runs) - each cell format: latency ms | $/1k tokens
Model: rw-large-v1 (fp16)
Strategy: fixed-batch-4    p50:  62ms | 1.42   p95:  210ms | 1.42   p99:  560ms | 1.42
Strategy: dynamic-batch    p50:  58ms | 1.10   p95:  185ms | 1.10   p99:  460ms | 1.10
Strategy: sessionized     p50:  63ms | 1.00   p95:  160ms | 0.98   p99:  370ms | 0.98

Model: rw-7b-q4 (quant)
Strategy: fixed-batch-4    p50:  55ms | 0.98   p95:  260ms | 0.98   p99:  710ms | 0.98
Strategy: dynamic-batch    p50:  50ms | 0.72   p95:  220ms | 0.72   p99:  520ms | 0.72
Strategy: sessionized     p50:  54ms | 0.68   p95:  180ms | 0.65   p99:  410ms | 0.65

Interpretation of table:
- Quantization materially lowers cost/1k tokens (seen in $ column) but increases tail latency under slotized fixed batching; when combined with session affinity the tail penalty largely disappears because KV cache hits short-circuit compute.
- Dynamic-batch reduces average latency and cost by filling slots efficiently but still leaves some tail due to contention during the 5s microburst peaks.
- Sessionized approach trades a small p50 uptick (prefetch overhead) for much better p95/p99 under surges. That trade is favorable for interactive SLAs.

ASCII sparkline: p99 latency across 10-minute window (sampled every 10s) for rw-7b-q4
Timeline: 0m------------5m------------10m
fixed-batch-4:  |___/\_____ /\_____ /\___/\_______|  (p99 peaks: 700->720->710ms)
dynamic-batch:  |__ /\___/\_/\___/\___/\__|       (p99 peaks: 520->560ms)
sessionized:    |_ /\_ /\__// _/\_ /\_ /\___|       (p99 peaks: 410->430ms)

Micro-observation: KV cache hit-rate distribution during surges (sample):
- sessionized: median 72%, 95th 88%
- dynamic-batch: median 38%, 95th 61%
- fixed-batch: median 12%, 95th 25%
Notes: The prefetch + affinity heuristic used in sessionized runs actively restored KV entries for warm sessions at arrival which explains the high hit rates.

Cost breakdown sketch (normalized compute units per minute during surge window):
- fixed-batch-4: baseline compute 1.0, idle/waste 0.45, prefetch 0.00 => effective compute 1.45
- dynamic-batch: baseline 0.82, idle/waste 0.22, prefetch 0.03 => effective compute 1.07
- sessionized: baseline 0.90, idle/waste 0.06, prefetch 0.08 => effective compute 1.04

Practical takeaway (for product):
- For chat products with bursty arrival patterns, prioritize sessionized routing + lightweight prefetch; it gives best tail control and cost-efficiency when KV reuse is expected.
- Reserve fixed small slots only for extremely latency-sensitive single-shot APIs; otherwise they inflate cost during bursts.
- Quantization should be paired with session affinity and a short prewarm window to avoid tail regressions.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) How does sessionized perf change when KV reuse drops below 30% (simulate multi-user interleaving)? Need an experiment with lower reuse.
2) Evaluate H100 pool differences: early H100 runs show slightly better p50 but cost delta vs A100 matters; run full price-normalized sweep.
3) Sensitivity to surge pulse shape: shorter 1s microbursts vs 5s pulses. Does tiling/slotization pivot matter?

Appendix: useful quick charts and commands used:
- loadgen config: bench/surge/profile_v3.yaml (attached in linked artifacts)
- trace query snippet used for KV hit-rate: SELECT ts,kv_hit,latency_ms FROM traces WHERE experiment = 'surge-apr21'
- baseline cost conversion: 1 compute-unit = $0.00085 per minute on A100 during contract period

Action items:
- [Priya] run low-kv-reuse sweep and attach outputs to this doc (JIRA INF-418).
- [Miguel] price-normalized H100 runs and update cost columns by 2028-04-28.
- [Ethan] draft one-pager for PM recommending sessionized default for chat tier; include p95/p99 focus.

Notes-to-self: preserve raw trace dumps, keep a copy of cold-run data separate. This draft is intended for the observability + serving-runtime sync next week.
